```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

How do supplier consolidation and retailer integration interact in one merger?
This guide calibrates four linked products and reports a hybrid merger's prices,
quantities and concentration. It needs `vertical` 0.3.0 and compatible `antitrust`
(at least 0.99.43). It uses public installed APIs, small in-memory inputs and no
optional `trade` installation or estimation toolchain.

## Calibrate a coherent four-product market

Each physical product passes from a supplier to its retailer. The input margin
at each tier is that tier's operating profit per unit divided by **its own
price**. The retailer margin is after paying the wholesale price. A wholesale
price is a transfer within the chain, not an additional physical production cost.

The example chooses Logit price sensitivity -1 and independent firms. Their
dollar markup is `1 / (1 - share)` at each tier. Equal tier markups imply
bargaining power .5 here; these are teaching choices, not universal defaults.

```{r market}
shares <- c(.15, .20, .12, .18)
markup <- 1 / (1 - shares)
cost_up <- c(1, 1.2, .9, 1.1)
cost_down <- c(.5, .6, .4, .55)
prices_up <- cost_up + markup
prices_down <- prices_up + cost_down + markup
owners_up <- c("U1", "U2", "U3", "U4")
owners_down <- c("D1", "D2", "D3", "D4")
labels <- c("one", "two", "three", "four")
fit <- vertical::calibrate(
  "logit", conduct = "vertical_bargaining",
  prices = prices_down, shares = shares, margins = markup / prices_down,
  ownerPre = owners_down, pricesUp = prices_up,
  marginsUp = markup / prices_up, ownerPreUp = owners_up,
  insideSize = 65, labels = labels
)
costs <- vertical::calcMC(fit@model, preMerger = TRUE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(product = labels, supplier_cost = costs$up,
                        retailer_cost = costs$down), digits = 4,
             caption = "Recovered physical costs (currency per unit).")
```

Product shares sum to .65, leaving outside share .35. `insideSize=65` means
65 physical inside units; the implied total market size is 100 for this example.
The recovered costs should match the positive supplied construction costs.
The price scale, marginal costs and dollar markups use the same currency per
physical unit. Margins such as .25 mean 25%, not .25 currency units.

```{r calibration-accounting}
stopifnot(
  max(abs(costs$up - cost_up)) < 1e-5,
  max(abs(costs$down - cost_down)) < 1e-5,
  abs(sum(vertical::calcQuantities(fit@model, preMerger = TRUE)) - 65) < 1e-5
)
```

The wrapper `fit` retains the observations and calibrated primitives;
`fit@model` is the linked structural model. These checks validate this example's
input/cost accounting; the package's independent bargaining/FOC tests supply
additional economic verification.

## Change both tiers' ownership

Merge the first two suppliers and give their owner the first two retailers.
The same label across tiers encodes common control; `"U1"` has no intrinsic
economic meaning beyond those relationships. The other two links remain
independent.

```{r hybrid}
result <- vertical::simulate(
  fit,
  ownerPost = list(up = c("U1", "U1", "U3", "U4"),
                   down = c("U1", "U1", "D3", "D4"))
)
vertical::merger_type(result)
pre <- vertical::calcPrices(fit@model, preMerger = TRUE)
post <- vertical::calcPrices(result, preMerger = FALSE)
price_table <- data.frame(
  product = labels, wholesale_pre = pre$up, wholesale_post = post$up,
  retail_pre = pre$down, retail_post = post$down
)
knitr::kable(price_table, digits = 4,
             caption = "Retail prices and wholesale transfers (currency per unit).")
```

Products one and two now pass between units of the same owner. Their wholesale
entries are **internal transfers**: the model pins them down using zero upstream
operating margin, so they equal upstream physical cost in this no-policy case.
These are not independently negotiated market-price forecasts for the integrated
links. Zero upstream operating margin does not mean the combined owner earns
zero profit; profit can appear downstream. Assess these links using retail
prices and combined owner/chain profits, rather than quoting an internal
wholesale-price reduction as a stand-alone competitive benefit.

This is a hybrid merger: it creates both same-tier consolidation and cross-tier
integration. Integration can change double-markup incentives while consolidation
changes competition; the net retail effect is an equilibrium outcome, not a
universal price-decrease or price-increase result. The originating fit remains
available for another scenario.

```{r quantities-concentration}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  product = labels,
  quantity_pre = vertical::calcQuantities(fit@model, preMerger = TRUE),
  quantity_post = vertical::calcQuantities(result, preMerger = FALSE)
), digits = 4, caption = "Physical quantities: one flow through both tiers.")
hhi_pre <- vapply(c("upstream", "downstream"), function(tier)
  vertical::hhi(result, preMerger = TRUE, revenue = FALSE,
                insideonly = TRUE, tier = tier), numeric(1))
hhi_post <- vapply(c("upstream", "downstream"), function(tier)
  vertical::hhi(result, preMerger = FALSE, revenue = FALSE,
                insideonly = TRUE, tier = tier), numeric(1))
knitr::kable(data.frame(tier = names(hhi_pre), pre = hhi_pre, post = hhi_post,
                        change = hhi_post - hhi_pre), digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "HHI: inside-only physical-quantity shares, 0–10000 scale.")
```

Read HHI by tier: the merger changes the supplier and retailer control
relationships. Here HHI is `10000 * sum(firm_inside_share^2)`, where each firm's
share sums its products' physical quantities and divides by total **inside**
quantity in that state. It excludes the outside option and uses quantity, not
revenue, weights. Computing it directly from the unconditional shares `.15`,
`.20`, `.12`, `.18` without first conditioning on their sum would give a different
index. The pre/post comparison above includes changed output shares as well as
changed ownership. Equal tier values in this example follow the same product
partition into owners; they do not establish that supplier and retailer market
definitions always coincide.

Physical output passes through both tiers; adding supplier and
retailer quantities would double-count the same units. When reporting welfare,
use producer surplus and consumer surplus measures with their stated price and
market-size conventions, rather than treating wholesale spending as an extra
social cost.

## Inspect calibration diagnostics and supported routes

```{r diagnostics-registry}
knitr::kable(vertical::calcDiagnostics(fit), digits = 6)
registry <- vertical::supportedModels()
knitr::kable(registry[, c("demand", "variant", "calibrate", "specify", "simulate")],
             row.names = FALSE, caption = "Registered vertical_bargaining models.")
```

Calibration diagnostics compare fitted and supplied inputs. They help reveal
inconsistent observations; finite prices or a small input discrepancy alone do
not prove a counterfactual satisfies every economic FOC. The independent
economic tests check portfolio bargaining and welfare identities separately.
The market-elasticity comparison is `NA` here because no observed market
elasticity was supplied; it is not a zero-elasticity finding.

Only three complete registry routes are implemented: standard Logit, standard
nested Logit (supply `nests`), and flat Logit second-score auction, all with
`vertical_bargaining` conduct. They are not a menu of arbitrary demand-by-conduct
combinations. Different models also change outside-option and allocation
interpretations; consult their help before replacing this specification.

| Operation | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| `calibrate()` | Recover primitives from linked observed inputs |
| `simulate()` | Solve a scenario using the fitted state |
| `update(fit, ...)` | Recalibrate revised observations under the same model |
| `counterfactual()` / `add_step()` | Describe supported scenario/path changes |
| `specify()` / `respecify()` | Unsupported for these vertical registry models |

For this fitted-state route, `ownerPost` must provide both `up` and `down`
ownership vectors of the fitted product lengths. Ownership matrices/partial
ownership are not accepted by this simulation interface; do not replace a
partial-control model with labels as an undocumented approximation. A positive
`mcDelta` is a proportional cost increase; a negative value is a reduction.

Known reporting caveat: nested Logit's market-elasticity report inherits an
inside-share normalization discrepancy from the inner model; its demand
derivatives and equilibrium calculations retain their existing definitions.
This Logit example does not fix or exercise that nested reporting issue.

instead; built bundles also provide
`vignette("vertical-tariffs-quotas", package = "vertical")`.
See `?vertical::calibrate`,
`?vertical::vertical.barg` and `?vertical::merger_type` for argument/reference
details. The economic framework is described in Sheu and Taragin (2021),
*RAND Journal of Economics*, 52:596-632, doi:10.1111/1756-2171.12385.
